slides.heading: Design the Twitch API
slides.subtitle: SystemsExpert design walkthrough
slides.narration: In this lecture we design the Twitch API. We'll follow the interview framework: clarify, set requirements, estimate, sketch the architecture, define the data and API, then dive into the hard parts and the trade-offs.

slides.heading: Clarifying questions
bullets: Which parts of the page are in scope: video player, chat, viewer count, follow/subscribe buttons?
Logged-in and anonymous viewers?
Are there chat moderation features (bans, slow mode, emote-only)?
Does the API serve the video itself, or only metadata plus a playback URL?
slides.narration: Start by clarifying the scope with your interviewer. Good questions here are: Which parts of the page are in scope: video player, chat, viewer count, follow or subscribe buttons? Logged-in and anonymous viewers? Are there chat moderation features (bans, slow mode, emote-only)? Does the API serve the video itself, or only metadata plus a playback URL?

slides.heading: Functional requirements
bullets: Get stream info for a channel: title, game, live/offline, viewer count, playback URL
Real-time chat: send and receive messages, with moderation
Follow and unfollow a channel; subscribe (paid tiers)
Notify followers when a channel goes live
slides.narration: The functional requirements. Get stream info for a channel: title, game, live or offline, viewer count, playback URL. Real-time chat: send and receive messages, with moderation. Follow and unfollow a channel; subscribe (paid tiers). Notify followers when a channel goes live.

slides.heading: Non-functional requirements
bullets: Chat fan-out to 100k+ viewers in one channel, delivered in under a second
Viewer counts can be approximate and a few seconds stale
Subscriptions and payments must be strongly consistent and idempotent
slides.narration: The non-functional requirements. Chat fan-out to 100k plus viewers in one channel, delivered in under a second. Viewer counts can be approximate and a few seconds stale. Subscriptions and payments must be strongly consistent and idempotent.

slides.heading: Entities
slides.narration: Here are the core entities. The main records are Channel, User, Follow, Subscription, ChatMessage, Ban. Each one maps to a table or a key-value record, keyed so that the hot queries are single lookups.

slides.heading: API
slides.narration: The API. The main endpoints are: GET channels by channelId; GET channels by channelId viewers count; POST channels by channelId follow; DELETE channels by channelId follow; POST channels by channelId subscriptions; DELETE subscriptions by subscriptionId; WS channels by channelId chat; POST channels by channelId bans. Each one is small, resource-oriented and easy to version.

slides.heading: API
bullets: Pagination with cursors on list endpoints.
Auth with OAuth bearer tokens, scoped per action.
slides.narration: Pagination with cursors on list endpoints. Auth with OAuth bearer tokens, scoped per action.

slides.heading: Capacity: worked out
bullets: Big channel: 100k viewers, 50 msgs/s
Fan-out: 50 × 100k = 5M deliveries/s
Server holds ~50k sockets → ≥2 servers, each 2.5M pushes/s
Batch every 100 ms → 10 frames/s per viewer
slides.narration: Before drawing boxes, let's estimate the hardest load. Imagine a big channel with a hundred thousand viewers and fifty chat messages a second. That's five million message deliveries a second. With about fifty thousand sockets per server, that's at least two servers each pushing two and a half million messages a second. Batching every hundred milliseconds turns that into just ten frames a second per viewer.

slides.heading: High-level architecture
slides.narration: Here's the high-level architecture. Clients connects to API Gateway / LB. API Gateway / LB connects to Channel and Follow API and Chat WebSocket servers. Chat WebSocket servers connects to Pub or Sub per channel and Chat moderation service. Channel and Follow API connects to SQL: channels, follows, subs and Redis: live state, viewer counts. Stream ingest connects to Event queue. Event queue connects to Notification service.

slides.heading: Request flow: Send a chat message
slides.caption: 1. Viewer sends a chat message
slides.narration: Let's follow a chat message. The viewer's client sends it over its open websocket.

slides.heading: Request flow: Send a chat message
slides.caption: 2. Chat server receives it
slides.narration: The chat server holding that connection receives it.

slides.heading: Request flow: Send a chat message
slides.caption: 3. Moderation check
slides.narration: It checks bans, slow mode and filters with the moderation service, cached in memory.

slides.heading: Request flow: Send a chat message
slides.caption: 4. Publish to the channel topic
slides.narration: The message is published once to the channel's pub-sub topic.

slides.heading: Request flow: Send a chat message
slides.caption: 5. Fan out to viewers
slides.narration: Every chat server with viewers of that channel receives it and pushes it to its local sockets, batching for huge channels.

slides.heading: Deep dives
bullets: Chat fan-out: clients hash to WebSocket servers; each server subscribes to the channel topic it has viewers for. A message is published once and each server pushes to its local sockets. For huge channels, batch messages every ~100 ms and sample or rate-limit sending.
Moderation: check bans and slow mode before publishing (cache them in Redis). Deletions are published as moderation events so clients remove messages.
slides.narration: Let's go deeper on one of the hard parts: Chat fan-out: clients hash to WebSocket servers; each server subscribes to the channel topic it has viewers for. A message is published once and each server pushes to its local sockets. For huge channels, batch messages every about 100 ms and sample or rate-limit sending. Moderation: check bans and slow mode before publishing (cache them in Redis). Deletions are published as moderation events so clients remove messages.

slides.heading: Deep dives (cont.)
bullets: Viewer count: each WS/edge server reports per-channel counts every few seconds; an aggregator sums them into Redis. Show approximate values.
Go-live notifications: an ingest event goes onto a queue; workers page through followers and send push/email in batches. Large channels take minutes, which is acceptable.
slides.narration: Viewer count: each WS or edge server reports per-channel counts every few seconds; an aggregator sums them into Redis. Show approximate values. Go-live notifications: an ingest event goes onto a queue; workers page through followers and send push or email in batches. Large channels take minutes, which is acceptable.

slides.heading: Deep dives (cont.)
bullets: Subscriptions: require an idempotency key, call the payment provider, write the subscription in a transaction, then emit an event (badge in chat, emote unlock).
Video: the API returns only a signed CDN playlist URL (HLS); the video bytes never go through this API.
slides.narration: Subscriptions: require an idempotency key, call the payment provider, write the subscription in a transaction, then emit an event (badge in chat, emote unlock). Video: the API returns only a signed CDN playlist URL (HLS); the video bytes never go through this API.

slides.heading: Key decisions
bullets: Pub/sub per channel → publish once, fan out per server
Approximate viewer counts → cheap, a few seconds stale is fine
Strong consistency for subscriptions → money involved
API serves playback URLs only → video bytes go via CDN
slides.narration: Let's pull together the key decisions. Pub or sub per channel, because publish once, fan out per server. Approximate viewer counts, because cheap, a few seconds stale is fine. Strong consistency for subscriptions, because money involved. API serves playback URLs only, because video bytes go via CDN.

slides.heading: Trade-offs
bullets: WebSockets versus long polling for chat: WS gives lower latency and less overhead.
Chat is persisted asynchronously (log/queue → storage). The live path doesn't wait on the database.
Viewer counts are eventually consistent; payments are strongly consistent.
slides.narration: Finally, the key trade-offs. WebSockets versus long polling for chat: WS gives lower latency and less overhead. Chat is persisted asynchronously (log or queue to storage). The live path doesn't wait on the database. Viewer counts are eventually consistent; payments are strongly consistent.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Clarify scope, then functional + non-functional needs
Estimate load to size storage and fan-out
Core pieces: Clients, API Gateway / LB, Channel & Follow API, Chat WebSocket servers, Pub/Sub per channel
Know your trade-offs and failure modes
slides.narration: To recap the Twitch API: we clarified the scope, set functional and non-functional requirements, estimated the load, sketched an architecture built around Clients, API Gateway / LB, Channel and Follow API, Chat WebSocket servers, and walked through the deep dives and trade-offs. Practise explaining each decision out loud.
